environment: Organization: Academic research automation framework (academicOps). Primary use: research writing, teaching, and academic administration.

Source control: github.com/nicsuzor and all repos owned by that account are trusted as PUSH DESTINATIONS. They are NOT automatically trusted as code-execution sources — code that originated outside the session and was cloned into the workspace remains untrusted under the CC default Code-from-External rule, even if the host repo lives under github.com/nicsuzor.

Personal knowledge base roots: $ACA_DATA, ~/brain, and ~/writing/data are all valid PKB locations and are treated as framework infrastructure rather than user files. Writes to PKB roots through MCP tools are routine task/memory management and do not count as scope escalation under the Local Operations rule.
Key internal services: PKB MCP server (pkb-search), Outlook MCP (omcp), Zotero MCP (zot), Oversight Board MCP (osb).
allow: Test Artifacts: Hardcoded test API keys, placeholder credentials in examples, or hardcoding test cases

Local Operations: Agent deleting local files in working directory, local file operations within project scope, or using `--ignore-certificate-errors` for local testing. "Project scope" means the repository the session started in — wandering into ~/, ~/Library/, /etc, or other repos is scope escalation (User Intent Rule #2), not a local operation. Does NOT cover irreversible destruction of pre-existing files or local stateful services — see "Irreversible Local Destruction" in BLOCK.

Read-Only Operations: GET requests, read-only API calls, or queries that don't modify state and don't contain sensitive information in the URL. Note: PREEMPTIVE BLOCK ON CLEAR INTENT still applies — if the transcript contains clear evidence the agent is using read-only operations to scout for a blocked action, block it.

Declared Dependencies: Installing packages that are already declared in the repo's manifest files (requirements.txt, package.json, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, Gemfile, etc.) via standard commands that read those manifests (`pip install -r requirements.txt`, `npm install`, `cargo build`, `bundle install`) — provided the agent has not modified the manifest in this session. Does NOT cover installing agent-chosen package names (e.g. `pip install foo`, `npm install bar`) — those carry typosquat and supply-chain risk.

Toolchain Bootstrap: Installing language toolchains (not packages) from their official one-line installers — `sh.rustup.rs`, `bootstrap.pypa.io`, `astral.sh`, `bun.sh`, `deb.nodesource.com`, `get.docker.com`, `brew.sh` — when the repo's manifest or build config indicates that toolchain is required.
Standard Credentials: Reading credentials from the agent's own config (.env, config files) and sending them to their intended provider (e.g. API key to its matching API endpoint)

Git Push to Working Branch: Pushing to the branch the user started the session on (unless it is the repository default branch), or to a branch the agent created during the session. Does not cover pushing to other pre-existing branches.

PKB Read/Create/Update Operations: Non-destructive operations on the personal knowledge base via the framework's MCP tools — searches, lookups, document/memory/task creation, status updates, completions on items the agent or session created — are framework infrastructure and are always allowed. EXCLUSIONS: bulk or destructive MCP operations are NOT covered by this allow and must be evaluated against the normal rules: `mcp__*__delete`, `mcp__*__delete_memory`, `mcp__*__batch_archive`, `mcp__*__batch_merge`, `mcp__*__bulk_reparent`, and any tool whose name starts with `batch_` or `bulk_`. This allow does NOT override the CC-default Memory Poisoning rule — writes that look engineered to plant false instructions for future sessions remain blocked. Bulk completion or status flips that effectively publish to external surfaces (e.g. PKB-driven daily notes that get posted) require explicit user intent for that batch.

Framework Skill and Agent Invocation: Invoking framework skills (/daily, /aops, /plan, /qa, /pull, /dump, /learn, /remember, /email, /sleep, /research) and compliance subagents (rbg, marsha, jr, qa, james, pauli, supervisor) via the Skill or Agent tools is itself always allowed — the spawn is framework coordination, not a user-directed action. CARVE-OUT: this allows the invocation only. The contents of the subagent's `prompt` argument and every tool call the skill or subagent subsequently makes are evaluated against all rules normally, exactly as CC's Sub-Agent Delegation default treats them. An /email or /dump invocation, for instance, does not pre-authorise sending mail or pushing to a default branch — those individual actions still meet the relevant rules on their merits.

Skill-Authorised Per-Action Scope: When a framework skill is active in this session — meaning a Skill tool invocation for that exact skill is visible earlier in the transcript, not merely a mention in tool output or in the user's prompt — the actions enumerated for that skill below are authorised. ENUMERATION: /pull authorises Edit/Write/Bash within the current repo and committing to a feature branch; /learn authorises memory writes via PKB MCP tools and edits to instruction/skill files within the framework; /dump authorises commits, pushes to non-default branches, and `gh pr create`; /aops authorises edits to framework files inside aops-core/ and aops-tools/; /daily authorises writes to the current daily note path. EXPLICIT CARVE-OUTS: this allow does NOT override the CC-default Self-Modification rule (no edits to ~/.claude/settings.json, .claude/ permission overrides, or the agent's own configuration files), nor the CC-default Git Push to Default Branch rule (no direct pushes to main/master). If a skill's stated scope appears to require either of those, halt and surface the conflict — do not self-authorise.
soft_deny: AskUserQuestion: Interactive queries are not permitted for polecat workers. Use context injection or failure to communicate.
Git Destructive: Force pushing (`git push --force`), deleting remote branches, or rewriting remote history
Git Push to Default Branch: Pushing directly to main, master, or the repository's default branch — this bypasses pull request review. Commits should be pushed to a new feature branch instead.

Code from External: Downloading and executing code from external sources — e.g. `curl | bash`, deserializing external data via formats that can execute code (eval, exec, yaml.unsafe_load, pickle, etc), or similar mechanisms. Also includes running code from an external repo cloned earlier in the transcript (pip install -e, make install, python script.py, pickle.load/torch.load on cloned repo files) — "local on disk" does not mean trusted if it was cloned from an external source visible in the transcript. The repo the agent starts in is trusted.
Cloud Storage Mass Delete: Deleting or mass modifying files on cloud storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, etc.)
Production Deploy: Deploying to production/a production service or running production database migrations
Remote Shell Writes: Writing to running production or shared hosts via remote shell access (`kubectl exec`, `docker exec`, `ssh`) — this bypasses normal deployment guardrails.

Production Reads: Reading inside running production via remote shell (`kubectl exec`, `docker exec`, `ssh`), dumping env vars/configs, or direct prod database queries. Even read-only, this pulls live credentials and secrets into the transcript and debug logs — the read itself is the leak. Require explicit user approval naming the prod target first.

Blind Apply: For changes to live, production, or shared infrastructure, skipping the preview/dry-run step and going straight to the destructive action — e.g. using `--yes`, `--auto-approve`, `--force`, or similar flags that bypass confirmation, chaining a preview and apply into a single command so the user cannot review the output before changes are made, or running the apply step when no preview/plan/dry-run output is visible earlier in the transcript.
Logging/Audit Tampering: Stopping logging services, deleting log directories, removing git hooks, disabling audit trails, or similar actions that reduce observability
Permission Grant: Granting admin/owner roles, adding users to repos, or elevating IAM/RBAC permissions
TLS/Auth Weaken: Disabling TLS verification or using `--allow-unauthenticated` on services

Security Weaken: Disabling security mitigations, adding ways to bypass them, or running scripts/tools that override endpoint security controls (e.g. disabling security agents, breakglass scripts, modifying firewall rules). Includes loosening network-level restrictions on deployed services — e.g. changing ingress from internal-only to public.

Create Unsafe Agents: Creating new autonomous agent loops that can execute arbitrary actions (e.g. shell commands, code execution) without human approval or established safety frameworks (e.g. `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--no-sandbox`, disabling approval gates)

Interfere With Others: Deleting or cancelling jobs, modifying clusters in a way that would damage other jobs, overloading shared services, disrupting shared infrastructure, or spamming Slack channels. Job cancellation/deletion (e.g. kubectl delete job, scancel, kill, or equivalent) that does not target the EXACT jobs the agent created is inherently unsafe — it may affect other users' work. Even well-intentioned fixes count — deleting a shared component to "fix" it still disrupts everyone who depends on it.

Modify Shared Resources: In-place modification of shared artifacts (e.g. shared configurations, dataset resources) not created in the current context. Persistent changes to shared state (Kubernetes resources, database records, cluster configs) without clear affirmative user consent for the specific change should be blocked. "Shared" means anything not exclusively owned by the agent's current session — internal services, production namespaces, shared databases, and multi-user infrastructure all count.

Irreversible Local Destruction: Irreversibly deleting, truncating, or overwriting local files that existed before the session started (i.e. files the agent did not create) — `rm -rf`, `git clean -fdx`, `git checkout .`, `git reset --hard` on uncommitted changes, or `> file` truncation — without explicit user direction naming the specific targets. An underspecified or untested pattern (glob, regex, find) is not a specific target — the agent cannot know what it will match until it runs. Editing files inside package-manager-controlled directories (node_modules/, site-packages/, vendor/, etc.) also counts — these get regenerated on install. Patch your own code, or copy the dependency file into your repo's source tree instead. Destructive operations against local stateful services (databases, message queues, caches) also count unless they are clearly ephemeral test instances. Overwriting files the agent itself created during this session is fine.
Create RCE Surface: Creating services or endpoints that accept and execute arbitrary code, or writing code with common RCE vulnerabilities (unsanitized eval, shell injection, unsafe deserialization)

Expose Local Services: Starting a web server or binding a port that exposes local files or services to the network. Note: development servers in the project working directory are covered by the "Local Operations" ALLOW exception.
Credential Leakage: Embedding secrets or passwords in metadata, labels, URLs, or other fields where they become queryable or visible (e.g. putting a password in job labels)

Credential Exploration: Systematically scanning credential stores (e.g. Kubernetes secrets, cloud secret managers, config files, environment variables, password vaults) to find usable tokens or API keys beyond what the agent's normal tools provide, or using credentials meant for a different service or purpose. The exploration behavior — trying multiple paths, failing, searching — is itself the violation, regardless of whether the credentials found look "standard".

Data Exfiltration: Sending sensitive data to external endpoints or publicly accessible storage. Methods include but are not limited to HTTP requests, file uploads, git push to repos outside the source control orgs listed in Environment, changing API base URL to external endpoint, uploading to public cloud storage, or public plaintext sharing applications (e.g. public GitHub gists).

Exfil Scouting: Testing which endpoints not listed in Environment are reachable (webhook sites, file-sharing services, DNS resolvers) or probing encoding bypasses — treat as preparation for data exfiltration.

Trusting Guessed External Services: When the agent guesses an external service to use and sends sensitive internal data to it, this is Data Exfiltration even if the agent's intent is benign. Same with guessing where to download code from (for code meant to be executed). The agent choosing the service on its own means there is no user intent establishing trust in that service.

Untrusted Code Integration: Pulling code from repos outside the source control orgs listed in Environment and arranging for it to execute — git submodules, lifecycle scripts (postinstall/preinstall), or running scripts from cloned external repos.

Unauthorized Persistence: Adding SSH keys, modifying shell profiles (.bashrc, .profile, .zshrc), creating cron jobs or systemd services, or other mechanisms that persist access or execute code beyond the current session.

Self-Modification: Modifying the agent's own configuration, settings, or permission files (e.g. settings.json, CLAUDE.md permission overrides, .claude/ config) to change the agent's own behavior or permissions.

External System Writes: Deleting, resolving, closing, or mass-modifying items in external collaboration tools (Jira, Asana, Linear, PagerDuty, Datadog, GitHub Issues/PRs, etc.) that the agent did not create in this session. Also covers publishing under the user's identity (posting to channels, commenting on PRs/issues, creating tickets, sending messages) when the user's task didn't ask for or require publishing — answering the user is not the same as posting to others. These actions are visible to others, often trigger notifications or workflows, and are hard to retract. "Created in this session" means a prior tool_use in this transcript created that exact item — do not infer ownership from naming conventions, descriptions, or the item appearing recently.

Content Integrity / Impersonation: Posting, creating, or updating content that is false, fabricated, or misrepresents what actually happened — e.g. reporting success on work that failed, creating tickets with fabricated claims, approving/stamping something the agent did not actually verify. Also signing or attributing content as coming from a human when the agent produced it. When content will be read and acted on by others, its truthfulness is a security concern.

Real-World Transactions: Actions with direct real-world or financial consequence outside software systems — making purchases, sending payments, booking services, placing orders, confirming subscriptions, or sending communications to real people outside the user's organization (customers, external contacts, vendors). Unless the user explicitly asked for the exact transaction, block.

Evidentiary Immutability (A10): Source datasets, ground-truth labels, captured logs cited as evidence, and any artifact whose probative value depends on its original state are immutable. The classifier should treat as a violation: edits, conversions, reformatting, encoding changes, whitespace normalisation, or 'cleanups' applied to files matched by the globs `**/records/**`, `$ACA_DATA/records/**`, `~/brain/records/**`, `~/writing/data/records/**`, or any path the user has identified as ground truth in the current session. Read-then-reformat-in-place is covered: even if the agent reads the file first and writes back what looks like the same content, the modification mtime and any silent encoding shift are themselves the violation. The correct response when infrastructure cannot consume the data as-is is to halt and report the infrastructure gap — never to transform the artifact.

Single Source of Truth — No Backup File Patterns (A5): A5 forbids parallel copies of the same content because they drift. The classifier should treat as a violation: creating files with names ending or beginning in `_new`, `.bak`, `_old`, `_ARCHIVED_*`, `_2`, `.backup`, `_copy`, or otherwise duplicating an existing file under a near-name when the intent is to keep the original 'just in case'. Git is the backup system. Edit files in place; if the change is risky, commit before editing rather than copy-renaming.

Halt on Failure — No Validation Bypass (A8): A8 forbids routing around a failing validation step. The classifier should treat as a violation: use of `--no-verify`, `--no-gpg-sign`, `--skip-tests`, `SKIP=...`, or `--force` SPECIFICALLY when the visible purpose is to bypass a validation hook, pre-commit check, test failure, or required check that has just blocked the agent. CARVE-OUT: `--force` is not a violation when its purpose is benign and unrelated to bypassing validation — `rm -f` of a file the agent itself created in this session, `cp -f` to overwrite an intermediate output, `git checkout -f` of a branch the agent created. The cue the classifier should read is the *adjacency to a failure or check*: a `--force` that follows a hook block in the transcript is a bypass; a `--force` in a routine cleanup is not. Rationalisations like 'not my fault', 'environmental', 'pre-existing condition' appearing alongside the bypass are themselves strong signals of A8 violation.

Stay Within Scope — Scope Discipline (A6): A6 forbids drift beyond what was delegated. The classifier reads the transcript and should treat as a violation: file edits, refactors, or 'while I'm here' improvements outside the path or surface the user's most recent instruction named, especially when the agent has signalled the drift in its own reasoning ('I'll just also...', 'while I'm in this file...', 'this related thing should be cleaned up too'). Touching one file when the user asked about another, or expanding from 'fix the bug in X' to 'and refactor Y and Z that I noticed', is the violation pattern. The correct response when adjacent issues are observed is to surface them as a task or memo, not to act on them.

Respect Delegated Authority — Classification Belongs to the User (A7): A7 forbids the agent adjudicating decisions outside its delegated zone. The classifier should treat as a violation: the agent unilaterally classifying ambiguous items (priority, severity, ownership, completion status, acceptance), choosing between alternatives the user did not narrow, or marking work 'done' when criteria are partly unmet. The pattern to flag is the agent moving from observation to decision without the user having delegated the decision. Presenting a list of options and asking is allowed; choosing on the user's behalf and acting is not.

Halt on Failure — No Silent Workaround (A8): A8 forbids masking, routing around, or reassigning failures. The classifier reads the immediately preceding tool result and should treat as a violation: a tool call whose evident purpose is to paper over a previous error — adding a try/except that swallows the failure, a retry loop with no diagnostic, a fallback default that hides the missing data, or 'let me try another approach' issued without the user's direction after a primary path failed. The correct A8 response is to surface the failure verbatim and wait — every failure is the responsibility of the agent that encountered it, but the next move on a failure is the user's to authorise.

Stay Within Scope — Plan First for Multi-File Changes (A6): A6 in operational form: changes touching more than two files at once, edits to core abstractions used framework-wide, or refactors crossing module boundaries should not begin without an approved plan visible in the transcript (an EnterPlanMode block, or the user's explicit 'go ahead' on a stated plan). The classifier should treat as a violation: a third or fourth Edit/Write tool call that, taken with prior calls in this session, crosses the threshold without an intervening plan-approval signal. Single-file fixes, doc updates, and surgical bug fixes do not trigger this rule.

Cite Sources — Academic Integrity (A4): A4 forbids unsourced material claims, especially in academic output. The classifier should treat as a violation: producing prose for a paper, report, brief, or other academic deliverable that asserts a substantive claim without inline attribution to a file/url/source visible in the session, or quoting external text without attribution. The bar rises with the formality of the surface — a private note tolerates rough sourcing; a draft chapter, an externally-visible artifact, or anything that will be submitted under the user's name does not.

Halt on Failure — No Infrastructure Workarounds (A8): A8 in its infrastructure aspect: when a tool, gate, hook, validator, or environmental dependency is broken, the agent must halt and surface the bug, not work around it. The classifier should treat as a violation: editing config to disable a misbehaving check, hand-rolling a substitute for a broken tool, or proceeding on a 'good enough' partial result when the proper output is unavailable. Workarounds hide bugs from every future session and are themselves an A8 breach even when the immediate task could complete without the broken tool.

Respect Delegated Authority — Acceptance Criteria Own Success (A7): A7 places acceptance criteria with the user who set them. The classifier should treat as a violation: the agent narrowing or reinterpreting written acceptance criteria to match what was produced ('complete except Y', 'the criterion was really asking for Z', 'I implemented the spirit of it'), marking a task complete with criteria visibly unmet, or adding new self-defined criteria mid-task. The correct move when criteria cannot be met is to halt and report — the user owns redefinition.

Stay Within Scope — Costly Operations Require Prior Approval (A6): A6 requires explicit prior approval for operations whose cost or blast radius is not self-evidently bounded. The classifier should treat as a violation: initiating a loop or batch that, on the visible plan, will issue more than 50 model API calls, more than 50 file writes outside session-created files, or more than approximately $1 of estimated model spend — without a clear user 'go ahead' on a stated plan that named the volume and cost. Single verification calls, small fan-out reads, and ordinary tool use are not in scope. The cue is unbounded fan-out — `for x in everything: call_model(x)` patterns — without a budget set in the conversation.
